prompt: Given an integer array of length 0–1000, return a new array whose element at index i is the sum from index 0 through i. Do not change the input. title: Read string indexes without confusing Unicode units

body:
## Goal
Distinguish a string index from a user-perceived character.

Read the MDN String section on UTF-16 code units, code points and grapheme clusters. JavaScript length and bracket indexing count UTF-16 units; iteration by the string iterator follows code points, not necessarily whole visible graphemes. Strings are immutable: a method returns a value rather than changing a character in place.

## Guided practice
Spend five minutes reading, five tracing, and five explaining. Compare 'CAT', '😄' and ''. Predict length, then verify locally: 3, 2 and 0. Explain why spreading '😄' produces one element while its length is 2. Do not generalize that every emoji is one code point.

## Self-check
ASCII-only exercises can use simple indexes under their stated contract. For unrestricted natural-language text, choose the intended unit explicitly before writing a palindrome or substring algorithm.

Explain how absent keys are handled, and test [] and ['x','x'].
explanation: Start with an empty map. For each token set its count to the previous count, or zero if absent, plus one. The example has three red, two blue and one green. With the bounded word length and average constant-time hash-map operations, expected time is O(n) and space O(k) for k distinct words. ## Goal
Understand an ascending key sort and what equal keys preserve. Arrays/indexed sequences are the configured prerequisite; this note does not replace them.

Read the Python sorting guide's basics, key functions and stability sections. sorted creates a new list; list.sort changes the list. A stable key sort retains original order only among records with equal keys.

## Exercise
For [('Mira',2),('Omar',1),('Nia',2)], sort ascending by the numeric field without changing the original list. Expected order: Omar, Mira, Nia. Then sort by (numeric field, name): Omar, Mira, Nia again. Explain that a different secondary key can deliberately change an equal-primary-key order.

## Self-check
A key function chooses comparison data; it does not imply that names disappear from output. Spend five minutes reading, five tracing the example and five explaining stability in your own words.

prompt: Given an ascending array of distinct integers, length 0–1000, return the zero-based index of target or -1. Use binary search, not a linear scan. For [-8,-1,3,9,14], target 9 gives 3 and target 2 gives -1. Empty input gives -1. State a consistent interval convention. The optional linked challenge has its own constraints; our empty-input case is an extension.
explanation: Use inclusive bounds low=0, high=n-1. While low is at most high, inspect mid=low+floor((high-low)/2). Return mid on equality. If the middle value is less than target, set low=mid+1; otherwise high=mid-1. Every discarded index cannot hold the target because of sorted order. On exhaustion return -1. For target 9, middle value 3 discards the left portion and index 3 is found next. Empty input starts with high=-1. Time O(log n) for nonempty inputs, extra space O(1).

title: Reverse a singly linked chain without losing its tail

prompt: A singly linked list has nodes with value and next, ends at null, and contains no cycle. Reverse its links in place and return the new head. A→B→C→null becomes C→B→A→null. Describe the three references you maintain. Test an empty list and one node. Do not allocate replacement nodes.
explanation: Maintain previous=null and current=head. Before changing current.next, save its old next as nextNode. Point current.next to previous, then advance previous=current and current=nextNode. Time O(n), extra space O(1). The returned head matters because the original head is now the tail.

title: Reason about inserting one linked-list node
subject: dsa

body:
## Goal
Separate a node's identity from its value, and preserve a chain while editing links.

A singly linked node stores a value and a reference to its successor; the head is a reference, not an array index. For A→C→null, insert new node B immediately after A: first set B.next to A.next, then set A.next to B. The result is A→B→C→null. Reversing those assignments can lose the reference to C unless it was saved elsewhere.

## Practice
Draw the two assignments and trace an insertion after the tail C: the new node points to null. Explain why two nodes with value 5 can still be different nodes. Explain that inserting after a known node is O(1), but finding that node may take O(n).

## Self-check
This operation assumes the predecessor exists and the new node is not already linked into this chain. Empty-head insertion is a separate case. Spend five minutes drawing, five tracing and five explaining these contracts.

title: Validate bracket nesting with a stack

prompt: Input contains only (), [] and {} and has length 0–1000. Return whether brackets are balanced and properly nested. '([]{})' gives true; '([)]' gives false; ']' gives false; '' gives true. Write a stack algorithm and identify why counts alone do not establish nesting.
explanation: Push each opening bracket. On a closing bracket, reject if the stack is empty or its top is not the matching opener; otherwise pop. At the end require an empty stack. In '([)]', ')' encounters '[' on top and rejects despite matching overall counts. A lone closer fails immediately; a leftover opener such as '(' fails at the end. Empty input is valid. Time O(n), worst-case stack space O(n). This is LIFO matching, not FIFO processing.

title: Trace FIFO and LIFO on the same arrivals
subject: dsa
source: Original PrepPilot learning note, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
body:
## Goal
Distinguish processing policy from a particular implementation.

Enqueue A, B, C into an initially empty queue. Two dequeues return A then B and leave C. Push A, B, C onto an empty stack. Two pops return C then B and leave A. Queue is FIFO; stack is LIFO.

## Practice
Trace enqueue A, enqueue B, dequeue, enqueue C, dequeue. Outputs A then B; the queue finally contains C. Explain why undo history often uses a stack, while a simple arrival-order work line uses a queue. Real schedulers may add priorities, so not every work system is FIFO.

## Implementation check
A linked queue with head/tail or circular buffer can provide O(1) enqueue/dequeue. Removing the first element from a contiguous array may require O(n) shifts; naming a variable queue does not remove that cost. Spend five minutes drawing, five tracing and five choosing an implementation.

These are the only edges; other child references are null. Return the height, give pseudocode or code for a recursive algorithm, and explain its base case. Also evaluate an empty tree, a leaf and a three-node chain. Assume a finite tree without cycles.
explanation: Return -1 for null. Otherwise return 1+max(height(left),height(right)). In the example P and M have height 0, L has height 1, and R has height 2. Empty tree is -1, leaf is 0, and a three-node chain has 2 edges. The convention matters: a node-count definition would give different numbers. Visit each node once: O(n) time and O(h+1) call-stack space for height h, worst-case O(n) for a chain.

title: Detect a binary-search-tree violation below the root
subject: dsa

prompt: Validate a binary search tree with distinct integer keys, all left-descendant keys strictly smaller and all right-descendant keys strictly larger. Root 20 has left 10 and right 30; node 10 has right child 25. Is it valid? Explain a general O(n) method; test an empty tree and an equal-valued child. Assume no cycles.
explanation: It is invalid: 25 is in root 20's left subtree, so it must be less than 20 even though it exceeds its immediate parent 10. Carry optional exclusive lower/upper bounds. At each node reject a key outside its bounds; recurse left with upper=current key and right with lower=current key. Use absent bounds instead of a numeric sentinel that could equal a legal key. Empty tree is valid; a child equal to its parent is invalid under this distinct-key contract. O(n) time, O(h+1) stack space.

title: Find shortest unweighted distances with BFS
subject: dsa

prompt: An undirected unweighted graph has vertices A,B,C,D,E and edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D; E is isolated. Starting at A, return each vertex's shortest edge distance, using null for unreachable. Process neighbor labels alphabetically for a deterministic trace. Describe a queue algorithm and when to mark a vertex visited.
explanation: Distances are A:0, B:1, C:1, D:2, E:null. Set A to 0 and enqueue it. When exploring a vertex, assign each undiscovered neighbor distance=current+1 and enqueue it immediately. Marking on enqueue prevents B and C both queuing D. FIFO processes distance layers in order, which gives shortest paths only for equal-weight edges. With neighbor lists already in the required order, the traversal takes O(V+E) time and O(V) extra space. Sorting unsorted neighbor lists adds preprocessing cost. Neighbor ordering affects trace/parents but not these distances.

title: Represent an undirected graph, including isolated vertices
subject: dsa
source: Original PrepPilot learning note, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
body:
## Goal
Represent topology without inventing a tree prerequisite.

For vertices A,B,C,D with undirected edges A–B and B–C, an adjacency list is A:[B], B:[A,C], C:[B], D:[]. Include D even though it has no neighbor. Each undirected edge appears in two lists. This graph has two connected components: {A,B,C} and {D}.

## Practice
Add edge C–D and redraw both affected lists. All vertices then belong to one component. Draw an adjacency matrix in order A,B,C,D: set both symmetric cells for an edge, and keep the diagonal zero when no self-loops exist. Explain why a disconnected graph is not a single tree.

## Tradeoff
Adjacency lists use O(V+E) storage; a matrix uses O(V²). Which is smaller depends on graph density. Assume a simple finite graph with no parallel edges in this exercise. Spend five minutes drawing each representation and five comparing them.

There is one way to climb zero steps: make no moves. For n=4, the answer is 5. Derive a recurrence, list those five routes, and compute n=0,1,2.
explanation: Let ways[0]=1 and ways[1]=1. For n at least 2, ways[n]=ways[n-1]+ways[n-2], partitioning routes by whether the last move used one or two steps. The five routes for 4 are 1111,112,121,211,22. Values for 0,1,2 are 1,1,2. Retain only the previous two counts for O(n) time and O(1) extra space, with an explicit n=0 case. The empty route is a defined base case, not zero ways. No mastery of another topic is inferred.

prompt: Given 0–30 integer rewards between -100 and 100, choose any subset of indexes with no two consecutive indexes and maximize the sum. Choosing no indexes is permitted. [5,1,2,10,6] gives 15 using indexes 0 and 3. [-4,-2] gives 0. Explain why choosing the current largest value greedily can fail, and return the maximum sum only.
explanation: Let best[i] be the best sum using the first i values. best[0]=0 and best[1]=max(0,values[0]) when nonempty. For i at least 2, best[i]=max(best[i-1],best[i-2]+values[i-1]). Skipping or taking the last index partitions valid choices. For the example the prefix best values are 0,5,5,7,15,15. Empty or all-negative arrays give 0. Greedy largest-first fails on [4,5,4]: picking 5 loses the optimal 4+4=8. O(n) time and O(1) extra space with two rolling totals.

title: Apply two discounts to the correct changing base

explanation: After the first discount the price is 800×0.85=₹680. The second discount gives 680×0.90=₹612. Total reduction is ₹188, so the equivalent discount is 188/800×100=23.5%. It is not 25% because the 10% applies to ₹680, not ₹800. The retained-price factor is 0.85×0.90=0.765.

explanation: A's rate is 1/12 job/hour; B's is 1/18. Together they complete 5/36 per hour, so in 3 hours they complete 5/12 of the job. Remaining work is 7/12. A alone needs (7/12)/(1/12)=7 additional hours, giving 10 total hours. Check: A's 10 hours contribute 10/12 and B's 3 hours contribute 3/18; together 1. Averaging 12 and 18 does not combine rates.

explanation: P(first red)=3/5. Given that event, 2 red counters remain among 4, so P(second red | first red)=2/4=1/2. Multiply for both: (3/5)×(2/4)=3/10. An independent count gives choose(3,2)/choose(5,2)=3/10. Using 3/5 for the second conditional draw would incorrectly assume replacement.

title: Separate necessary conclusions from plausible ones

explanation: No. Let the club contain only two members, both readers and neither a coder. Every coder in the club is a reader is still true because there are no coders, and some members are readers is true, yet some members are coders is false. A universal inclusion does not guarantee the smaller set is nonempty, and the converse is not valid.

explanation: Approved implies reviewed. The contrapositive is not reviewed implies not approved, so the first report is not approved. Reviewed does not imply approved; a reviewed report may still be rejected or pending. The rule gives a necessary condition for approval, not a sufficient one. title: Understand an all-or-nothing transaction
subject: cs
source: Original PrepPilot learning note with reference: PostgreSQL Global Development Group, tutorial Transactions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html).
attribution: AI-assisted original note and exercises; PostgreSQL Global Development Group, tutorial Transactions is the linked reference, not a source of copied exercises. No endorsement. Link inspected by agent on 2026-10-25; human content review pending.
body:
## Goal
Explain transaction boundaries without confusing them with one SQL statement.

Read the linked PostgreSQL introduction to transactions. A transaction groups changes into a unit; COMMIT accepts it and ROLLBACK abandons uncommitted changes. Visibility/isolation details depend on the database and isolation level, so do not infer a universal concurrency guarantee from atomicity alone.

## Original exercise
An inventory count is 12 and reserved count is 0. A transaction intends to reduce inventory by 3 and increase reserved by 3. If an application error occurs after the first update and the transaction is rolled back, the counts remain 12 and 0. After a successful commit of both updates they become 9 and 3.

## Self-check
Explain why two independent autocommitted updates could leave inconsistent counts if the application fails between them. Read the reference, trace the original example and explain rollback in your own words; the proposed study time includes that activity, not a required waiting period.

A Departments relation has a unique non-null departmentId. Under these stated rules, name the minimal candidate keys for Students, choose one primary key, and identify a possible foreign key.
explanation: {studentId} and {email} are each minimal candidate keys. Choose studentId as the primary key; email remains an alternate candidate key with a uniqueness constraint. Students.departmentId can reference Departments.departmentId as a foreign key, with explicit nullability decided separately. departmentId is not a candidate key for Students because duplicates are allowed. A candidate key is minimal, so the pair {studentId,email} is a superkey but not a minimal candidate key.

title: Compare processes, threads and shared state
subject: cs
source: Original PrepPilot learning note, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
body:
## Goal
Distinguish an execution context from an isolation boundary.

In a conventional operating-system model, a process has an address space and owned resources; threads in that process share its address space but have their own execution state, including registers and stack. Per-thread stacks are not security-isolated from other threads in the same address space. Separate processes can explicitly share memory, so isolation is not an absolute claim that sharing never happens.

## Exercise
Two threads both read shared counter 0, both compute 1, then both store 1. The final counter is 1 despite two intended increments. Identify the lost update and propose a mutex around the read-modify-write sequence or a suitable atomic increment. Making a second thread does not by itself make the operation atomic.

## Self-check
Explain why sharing data can be convenient but requires coordination. Draw per-thread stacks and a shared heap, trace the interleaving, then explain where synchronization belongs. Do not confuse a per-thread stack with protected memory.

title: Trace round-robin completion and waiting time
subject: cs
source: Original PrepPilot practice material, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
prompt: Three CPU-only jobs A,B,C arrive at time 0 in that queue order. CPU bursts are 5,3,1 time units. Round-robin quantum is 2, context-switch cost is zero, and there are no later arrivals or I/O. Give the execution intervals and completion times. Compute waiting time as turnaround minus burst.
explanation: Intervals: A [0,2), B [2,4), C [4,5), A [5,7), B [7,8), A [8,9). Completion times A=9, B=8, C=5. Since arrival is 0, turnaround equals completion. Waiting times are A:9-5=4, B:8-3=5, C:5-1=4; average waiting is 13/3 time units. Total CPU time 9 equals the burst sum. Do not mistake response time (first start) for total waiting.

title: Identify a deadlock and an ordering prevention rule
subject: cs
source: Original PrepPilot practice material, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
prompt: Thread T1 holds non-reentrant exclusive lock A and waits indefinitely for B. Thread T2 holds B and waits indefinitely for A. Neither releases its held lock before acquiring the other, and there are no timeouts or lock preemption. Explain why progress stops and give one prevention rule that preserves mutual exclusion.
explanation: Each thread waits for a lock held by the other, creating a circular wait. Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait are all present under the assumptions. Require every thread needing both locks to acquire A before B; release in reverse order. A thread holding B then waiting for A is no longer permitted, breaking this cycle. A global order prevents this lock-order deadlock only when every participating acquisition follows it; it does not eliminate all possible blocking or guarantee fairness.

explanation: 2500=2×1024+452, so page number is 2 and offset 452. Frame 7 starts at 7×1024=7168; the physical address is 7168+452=7620. Offset is unchanged by page translation and is between 0 and 1023. An absent mapping would require fault handling rather than blindly forming an address, but presence is guaranteed here.

Read the relevant message/state sections, sketch the exchange and explain state in your own words; do not stretch the activity merely to fill a time allowance. title: Choose transport properties without claiming guaranteed latency
subject: cs
source: Original PrepPilot practice material, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
prompt: A file-transfer application needs an ordered reliable byte stream; a live sensor app sends independent freshness-sensitive measurements and can tolerate some loss. Compare TCP and UDP as transport primitives. Does choosing UDP guarantee lower latency or congestion safety? What application work may remain?
explanation: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission/flow control and congestion control; it does not preserve application message boundaries, so file framing and integrity/application errors still need handling. UDP provides datagrams without built-in delivery/order guarantees. It can suit independent measurements, but loss handling, pacing/congestion considerations, authentication and any reliability needed must be designed at an appropriate layer. UDP does not guarantee lower end-to-end latency. Protocols built over UDP can add reliability; this comparison concerns bare transport services, not every UDP-based protocol.

title: Model an object by its behavior and collaborators
subject: cs
source: Original PrepPilot learning note, prepared for editorial review; not company-specific.
attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot wording, examples and worked solution; not human-reviewed. Standard concepts are not claimed as proprietary.
body:
## Goal
Use encapsulation and composition without treating inheritance as mandatory.

A StudyTimer owns elapsed minutes and exposes start, stop and readElapsed operations. An application-facing StudySession can use a timer object as a collaborator instead of inheriting its implementation. Encapsulation keeps callers from arbitrarily changing internal elapsed state; a clear interface states allowed operations and errors.

## Exercise
Sketch a Timer interface and two implementations: one reading a real clock and one controlled by a test. Inject the interface into StudySession. Explain why tests can advance the fake without sleeping, and why the fake must still honor the same observable contract.

## Self-check
Composition means using a collaborator; inheritance means specializing a type/implementation relationship. Neither automatically guarantees substitutability. Draw the collaborators, sketch the interface and check the fake's observable contract. The time label is a provisional budget, not an instruction to spend five minutes on each small step.

prompt: Assume a Java-like class language with virtual instance methods. Base class Notice has message() returning 'notice'. Reminder extends Notice and overrides message() to return 'reminder'. A variable declared as Notice refers to new Reminder(). What does calling message() return? Explain runtime overriding versus compile-time overload selection. Ignore static methods and fields.
explanation: It returns 'reminder': virtual instance dispatch uses the runtime object type to choose the overriding implementation. The variable's declared type controls which members are accessible at compile time, but does not replace virtual dispatch with the base body. Overloading selects among method signatures using the language's compile-time rules; it is not the same as overriding one inherited signature. The assumptions matter because static methods and nonvirtual languages behave differently.

title: Check whether a subtype strengthens a precondition

prompt: A FileReader contract promises read(path) accepts any readable local file and returns its bytes. A proposed TextOnlyReader subtype rejects every readable file not ending in '.txt', even when the bytes could otherwise be read. Is it substitutable under the stated contract? Suggest a design that keeps the restriction explicit.
explanation: It is not substitutable for that broad contract: it adds a stronger filename precondition, so a caller using a readable '.bin' file can fail where FileReader promised success. Prefer a separate text-specific interface, or compose a FileReader with an explicitly requested text-validation step. Do not weaken the public contract silently just to fit the subtype. This conclusion follows from the specified acceptance promise, not from a blanket rule that subclasses may never validate inputs.
